blocks.text: The book put it flatly, the way it put everything.

WO-1-001 FLOOR 1. PUBLIC FLOOR. TIER 1. FAULT: CRACK. EAST STAIR, FOOTING TO FLOOR 4. CAUSE: UNDIAGNOSED. GRADE REQUIRED: 1. SYMPTOM: LOAD, CARRIED IN THE LEGS. STATUS: OPEN. ESCALATES EVERY 7 DAYS, TAKEN OR NOT. TAKEN BY:

The TAKEN BY line was still empty at five o'clock. I'd tried the pen again at noon, and again at four, the way you try a door you know is locked, and the book had stayed exactly as polite as before. Holding two. So when people started coming home I gave up on the office and went and stood at the foot of the east stair instead. If the stair couldn't have me on paper, it could have me on the bottom step.

The crack started there, under the first tread, a dark line you could have slid a bus ticket into. It crossed the tread, went up the stringer wall, and kept going round every turn to the fourth floor. It had stopped ticking about midday. I didn't like that any better.
Mrs Quarry came in first, with two bags from the market and her keys on a cord round her neck.
"Over the crack, Mrs Quarry," I said. "Then keep to the wall side. Left-hand edge of each tread, all the way up."
She stepped over it like it was a dog asleep. "Is it safe?"

"I'm watching it," I said. "It's in the plaster and the wall. I'm checking whether it's in the treads as well. The edges take the weight best." I coughed, and it came up grey. Five days I'd been breathing floor 6's soot, and my face was hot with its fever on top.
"The association will want to know what the Trust is doing."
"So will I," I said.

Gil Ferrabee came in with his bike on his shoulder, and I made him leave it in the lobby. Two lads from 3B came in with chips. I told every one of them the same thing: over the crack, wall side, edges. Nobody argued. People don't, when it's a stair.
When it was quiet I sat on the second step and put my hand flat on the tread above the crack, and talked to it, because it was there.

"I'm sorry," I said. "You should be on me by now. You'd be getting looked at properly instead of having people step over you with chips." The tread was cold under my burnt knuckles. "I'll have a free slot for you by tonight. That's a promise. Tonight."
Then I had to work out how.

At grade one I could hold two orders, and both of mine were floor 6. WO-6-003 was the hot run, the one with the fever, and I couldn't touch that until I had the right metal. WO-6-002 was the soot. I knew what was wrong with it, which was half the reason it had been driving me mad for five nights. At the end of the flue gallery there's a damper on a thin square spindle, and its handle had worn round inside. The handle spun, the damper hung nearly shut, and the smoke backed into the gallery and into me. The spindle didn't want a new handle. It wanted a key. Something with a good square socket.

Everything on floor 6 wanted grade two, and new metal is grade one whatever's stamped on it. I had a box of stamped brass lies in the office to prove that. I could have gone back to floor 5 for salvage, the way I had for the bracket, but salvage opens another order up there for me to carry, and the whole point was an empty hand.
So I needed something old that somebody would give me.

I went and knocked at 1C, because 1C backs onto the east stair and I wanted to know whether the crack had come through inside. Mr Tull opened the door in his cardigan, with the telly going behind him.
"It's the stair man," he said.
"Can I look at your wall, Mr Tull? The one by the stair."
He let me in. The crack hadn't come through. But his radiator was knocking like somebody in it wanted out, and there was a towel on the carpet and a radiator key in his hand.
It was brass, with a little butterfly grip worn smooth to the shape of a thumb. The square socket on the end had gone gold at the edges from turning.
"Been knocking since they drilled," he said. "All day."
"Air in it," I said. "Can I?"

He gave me the key and I knelt and bled it. Ordinary work. A hiss, a spit, a towel. The knocking stopped and the radiator went warm all the way across, and I sat back on my heels and coughed into my elbow.

"That's been my key fifty years this winter," said Mr Tull. "My wife bought it off the ironmonger on Mallow Street the first week we moved in. Every October since, I do the radiators. Nobody else has ever touched it."
I looked at the key in my hand and thought about the damper spindle, and the square on the end of it, and what fifty Octobers might come to.

"Mr Tull," I said, "I've got a job upstairs that wants a key like this. An old one. I can't get one new that'll do." I made myself say the rest. "Would you give me it? I'll bring you a new one tomorrow. I'll do your radiators myself, every October, if you want."
He looked at me for a while. He was eighty-something and he took his time over most things.
"Have it," he said. "Go on. You did the radiator, it's yours. I give it you." He pointed at the door. "And go and cough somewhere else, young man. You're putting me off my programme."
I thanked him three times on the way out. He shut the door on the third.

Nessa came down the east stair at about eight, on the wall side, on the edges, as if I'd told her. I hadn't. She had a plate under a cloth in one hand and the rail in the other, and at the first-floor landing she stopped, put the plate down on the step, and laid her palm flat on the crack.

She didn't look at it like a tenant. She looked at it the way I'd have looked at it. She followed it down with two fingers to the foot and squatted there, her knees cracking, and I thought she'd need a hand up and I didn't offer it.

"Not settling," she said. "Settling goes like a tree. Branches. This goes like a zip. They put holes in the footing a hand apart, here, here, here, and the brick opened from one hole to the next. Like a coat button pulling."
She was right. It had taken me twenty minutes that morning to be sure of it.
"Jurek was in the building trade?" I said. I'd been thinking it since the tap. Somebody had taught her to look at a wall.

"Jurek drove a tram for thirty-one years," she said. "He could not hang a picture. I hung the pictures." She pushed herself up on the rail and sat down on the third step, above the crack, with the plate on her knees. "I was in the trade, Mr Caretaker. Not his trade."
Down in the lobby Dusty lifted his head off the mat and looked at her.

"Sit," she said to me, so I sat on the step below. She took the cloth off the plate. Cabbage rolls, still warm. She gave me one and a fork, and I ate it, because I always do, and because it was the best thing that had happened since morning.
"For twenty-two years," she said, "every week, I write a letter about the caretaker of this building. To the Housing Commission. To a man there called the Clerk of Placements."
I had the fork halfway to my mouth.
"The rent tribunal people?"

"That is the window they show the street." She folded the cloth in quarters. "I wrote about Walter. Now I write about you. Since your first week. You read everything twice. You talk to the pipes. You eat what you are given. You go up in the service lift at night and come down coughing. All that, I wrote."
"Why?"

"Because that is my rent." She said it flatly. "My lease is cheap because I write. Before that, when I was young, I was a sweeper. We cleared the floors above this one, in buildings like this, when the city still did it with brooms and worse. When I got old they gave me a good lease and a pen. Twenty-two years."

My hand had gone into my pocket without asking me. Jurek's washer was in there, and the counterfeit jumper next to it, and I could have taken the washer out and asked her about the line in the book that said roll 4C in the old square capitals. I didn't. She'd given me one hard thing tonight already.
"Why tell me now?" I said.
She looked down the stairwell at the dog.

"Because he will tell you, if I don't," she said. "And I would rather you heard it in my voice than in his." Then she looked at the crack. "And because somebody did that with a drill, and I can read it, and I do not like to be on the wrong side of a thing I can read."

I didn't know what to say to her, so I asked about the footing. How deep she reckoned the holes went. Whether the brick had moved on both sides or one. She answered every question exactly, and neither of us said a word about the letters for ten minutes.
When the plate was empty she stood up.
"Think, Mr Caretaker," she said. "Then come and tell me what I write this week. I post it Friday." And she went back up, on the wall side, on the edges.
I took the plate down to the office, and Dusty came with me.

I opened the book to floor 6 and wrote WO-6-002's cause on its line, in my own hand: damper handle worn round on its spindle; damper hanging shut; flue backing into the gallery. Age. No party. I read it twice, slowly, lips moving, the way I read anything I'm putting my name near. Then I took the slip and Mr Tull's key and went to the lift.

For a fortnight Dusty had lain down on the tiles every night when I pressed 6, and I'd held the door and gone up alone. Tonight he got in. He sat against the back wall with his nose to the gap and sighed.
The doors opened on floor 6 and the heat came in, and the smell of coke, and he stood up and said, "Mind the gantry, son. Third plate from the end's loose."
"Did you know?" I said. "About her letters."
"Hold the door."
"Walter."

"I knew." He came out after me and sat at the top of the gantry steps. "She wrote on me every week for twenty-odd years. I knew from the first month. Building like this, there's always somebody writing on you. Better one you know."
"She's been feeding me. All that time."
"She feeds everybody," said Walter. "Fit your part."

The flue gallery runs along the back wall behind the furnace, low enough that I have to stoop, and every brick in it is furred black. The soot sat in my chest like wet wool. The furnace lodger made a low noise in the vents as I went past, the sound of something hungry trying to be patient. Its coal wasn't due for six days. I didn't stop.

At the far end the damper spindle stuck out of the flue like a thin grey finger. I took Mr Tull's key out of my pocket, and in my palm, right there at the fault, it was heavy. Heavier than the brass in it had any right to be. Like Jurek's tap had been on riser 2, like a full cup when you thought it was empty. I stood bent over in the soot with my eyes watering and just held it for a second, because it's the best thing my hands know.

I filed the spindle's end square again, where there was a good half-inch of square left under the rounding. The key's socket went on snug. I pinned it through and turned the butterfly grip, slowly, and felt the damper swing open inside the flue, and then the whole gallery took a breath. The draw came up through the bricks with a sound like a long sigh going the right way, and the soot that had been hanging in the air started going up instead of out. Behind me the lodger roared, pleased, and the furnace door glowed.
I signed the slip against the flue, on the brick, at the fault. TAKEN BY, my name. SIGNED OFF AT FAULT, my name again.
Down in the basement, the book would be going black.

The first breath after was the best breath I'd had in five days. My chest opened all the way down. I still had the fever from the hot run, and my face still burned, and my knuckles still stung in their stripes, but the grey was gone out of my lungs. I said, out loud, to the stair that was nowhere near me, "There. That's your slot." Promise kept.
Walter got back in the lift before me and lay down. I held the door open on floor 6, so he could talk if he wanted, and I did my thinking out loud, because that's how I do it.

"She lied to me for five months," I said. "No. She didn't tell me something for five months. That's different. Everyone in this building isn't telling me something. You aren't. I'm not telling anybody about Fennick." I hadn't meant to say that word in here and I went past it quickly. "She gave me Jurek's tap. She gave it, she didn't sell it. She told the association to wear their keys. She came down tonight and told me herself, before you could. A woman who wanted to keep writing about me in secret wouldn't have done that. She'd have kept writing." I wiped my face. It was wet with sweat and soot. "I'm going to keep trusting her. That's what I've decided. Not because she feeds me."
"No," said Walter.
"Partly because she feeds me."
He didn't argue.
"And the stair," I said. "I've got the slot. I'm going down to take it."

"Don't," said Walter. "Not yet." He lifted his head off his paws. "That stair's running whether you carry it or not. Taking it doesn't stop the clock, son. All it does is put it in your legs. Find out what it stands on first. Then take it, and know who you're putting it on."
He was right, and I could see why. A public floor runs its own clock. Carrying it early wouldn't buy the stair a day. It would only cost me my legs while I worked out the cause.
I let the doors go.
In the office the book had the floor 6 page open, and WO-6-002's line was black. Under the date, the header had moved.
CARETAKER: R. ANAND GRADE: 1 (ODD-JOB) CREDITS: 11 HOLDING: 1 CERTIFIED: 5
Holding one. It looked like a spare room. I turned back to the floor 1 page and put my finger on WO-1-001's empty TAKEN BY line, and left it empty, because I knew exactly why now.
Nessa came down to the basement at a quarter to twelve in her coat, with a writing pad and a pencil, and knocked on the office door frame even though it was open.
"You've decided," she said. It wasn't a question.
"Keep writing," I said. "Don't stop on my account. If you stop, they'll want to know why, and they'll send someone else to write about me, and I won't know who. I'd rather it was you."
She sat in Walter's old chair, and Dusty came and put his head on her shoe.

"I will keep writing," she said. "The lease is my home. Jurek's coat is by that door. I will not lose that door." She opened the pad. "But from tonight I write what we agree. Mostly I am on your side, Mr Caretaker. The rest of me pays rent."
"That's fair," I said, and it was.
"So. What do I say?"
"Say the stair's cracked. They know that already."
She wrote it.
"Say I've got a cough," I said.
"You coughed less tonight."
"Say I've got a cough," I said again, and she looked at me over the pad and wrote it. "Say I fixed Mr Tull's radiator."
"That is true."
"Most of it should be."

She wrote three more lines I didn't ask to see, and tore the page off, and folded it in four, and told me none of it was about floor 6. Then she went back up to bed, and I washed her plate in the office sink and left it on the desk for the morning.

I didn't sleep. I sat on the bottom step of the east stair with the fever in my face and my lungs clear for the first time since floor 6, and listened to the building breathe round me, and at six o'clock, with the light coming grey through the front door's glass, something came through the letterbox.

The oak door dragged when I opened it, on its dropped top hinge, and there was a white van pulling away from the kerb with the city's crest on the side. The envelope on the mat was addressed to the Caretaker, Pellory Court. Under that it said, in smaller type, copy to Greyfold Property Partners, attention I. Tarrant.
I read it twice on the doormat, lips moving.

It said the city had received notice of structural damage to the east stair of 14 Wickline Street. It said an inspection of the stair was booked for six o'clock in the morning, three days from today, and in case I was slow it said that too: in seventy-two hours. It said that if the stair failed, the conditions of the wrecking permit held over the building would apply.

I stood on the mat in the grey light with the letter in my hand and looked back at the crack under the first tread, and I had a free slot for it, and a clear chest, and three days, and no idea yet what that stair stood on.
